summary: A 1970 note by T. Schipper about reallocation in case of an input error. It concerns how space allocated for incoming data is handled when something goes wrong.

eli5.summary: What should a computer do with the space it saved for a message when something went wrong? This note thinks about that.

questions: reallocation in case of input error
what happens when a message is corrupted
how to recover from input errors
subtitle: How to recover buffer space when messages arrive with errors.

tldr.problem: When an input error occurs during message reception, the receiving NCP may not be able to determine the message length, leaving allocated buffer space in an undefined state.
tldr.mechanism: If an input error is detected and the link number is found, send GVB (frac=0) to the sender to stop transmissions on that link, disregard further messages, wait for RET, then issue a new ALL to resume.
tldr.outcome: The receiving NCP can realloc buffer space and resume transmission cleanly. The protocol ensures the link is clear before the new allocation is issued, preventing desynchronization.

today: RFC 71 is Unknown status. The procedure is specific to the ARPANET flow control scheme. Modern protocols handle errors through checksums and retransmission at higher layers, and flow control uses window-based mechanisms.

sections.title: The Error Recovery Problem
sections.content: Tjaart Schipper from UCLA-CCN describes a procedure for the UCLA CCN Host to use when recovering from input errors in flow control. If corruption or noise occurs during message reception from the IMP, the receiving NCP may be unable to determine where the message ends. This leaves the buffer allocation in an inconsistent state—space has been reserved but the message is incomplete.
sections.eli5: If a message gets garbled, the receiver does not know how much space it took up or whether the rest of the message is coming.

sections.title: Recovery Procedure
sections.content:
When an input error is detected and the intended link number can be identified, the receiving NCP takes the following steps:

First, send a GVB (with frac = 0) to the sending host, instructing it to stop transmissions on that link. Then disregard all further incoming messages on that link until the error is resolved.

The sending host's behavior depends on its state. If it is not waiting for an RFNM when the GVB arrives, it sends RET (return) immediately. If it is waiting for an RFNM corresponding to the message with the error, or an RFNM for a subsequent message, it sends RET only after the RFNM has been received. This ensures that in-flight messages are acknowledged before the link is considered clear.

Once RET is received, the receiving NCP issues a new ALL (allocation) on that link to begin accepting messages again.
sections.eli5: Say 'stop', wait for the other side to say 'OK I have stopped and saved my place', then tell them 'now you can send again'. This makes sure both sides agree the link is clean.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
This recovery procedure is essential for maintaining flow control consistency in the presence of errors. If a message arrives corrupted and the receiver does not know its true length, the pre-allocated buffer space becomes unusable—it is neither fully consumed nor available for new allocations. The GVB/RET/ALL sequence resynchronizes both hosts.

The key is waiting for in-flight RFNM acknowledgments before considering the link clear. This prevents the sending host from transmitting new messages while the receiver is in an undefined state.
sections.eli5: Both sides need to agree that things are OK again before continuing. It is like a handshake: 'stop?', 'stopped', 'thanks, we can restart now'.
